html:
A huge marble temple of the goddess Artemis at Ephesus, on the west coast of Anatolia, begun about 550 BCE. Its later rebuilding was counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

The first great temple was paid for in part by Croesus, the rich king of Lydia, who had taken Ephesus. It was among the first large Greek buildings made of marble, with a forest of tall columns. The Artemis worshipped here was a local mother goddess, shown with rows of egg shaped forms on her chest.

In 356 BCE a man named Herostratus burned it down to make his name famous; legend says it happened on the night Alexander the Great was born. The people of Ephesus rebuilt it even larger. Gothic raiders damaged it in the 200s CE, and as Christianity spread its stones were taken for other buildings. Today one rebuilt column stands in a marshy field. The philosopher Heraclitus is said to have left his book there.
sum: A huge marble temple of the goddess Artemis at Ephesus, on the west coast of Anatolia, begun about 550 BCE. Its later rebuilding was counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
